courses.title: Introduction to Pharmacy and Pharmaceutics
courses.description: The pharmacy profession in Nigeria, pharmaceutical calculations, the prescription, sources of drugs and introductory dosage-form science.

topics.title: The Pharmacy Profession in Nigeria
topics.summary: History, roles of the pharmacist, regulation and the pharmacy workforce.

material.heading: Roles and regulation
material.body: Pharmacists are custodians of medicines: they dispense, counsel patients, monitor therapy, manufacture and assure the quality of medicines, supply drug information and promote public health. Pharmacy practice in Nigeria is regulated by the Pharmacy Council of Nigeria (PCN), established by the Pharmacists Council of Nigeria Act (now the PCN Act 2022), which registers pharmacists and pharmacy technicians and licenses premises including patent and proprietary medicine vendors (PPMVs). The Pharmaceutical Society of Nigeria (PSN) is the professional association. The Doctor of Pharmacy (PharmD) is now the entry-level degree in Nigerian universities, replacing the BPharm.
keyPoints: PCN regulates pharmacy practice and licenses premises

material.heading: Areas of practice
material.body: Pharmacists work in community (retail) pharmacy, hospital pharmacy, industrial (manufacturing) pharmacy, regulatory agencies (NAFDAC, PCN), academia, the armed forces and public health programmes (e.g. HIV, TB, malaria supply chains). Pharmaceutical care, described by Hepler and Strand (1990), is the responsible provision of drug therapy to achieve definite outcomes that improve a patient's quality of life.

topics.title: Pharmaceutical Calculations
topics.summary: Units, dose calculations, percentage and ratio strengths, dilutions and paediatric doses.

material.heading: Units and concentrations
material.body: Metric units: 1 g = 1,000 mg; 1 mg = 1,000 µg (micrograms); 1 L = 1,000 mL. Percentage strength: w/v = grams per 100 mL (e.g. 5% dextrose = 5 g/100 mL); w/w = grams per 100 g; v/v = mL per 100 mL. Ratio strength expresses dilute solutions, e.g. 1:1,000 adrenaline = 1 g in 1,000 mL = 1 mg/mL; 1:10,000 = 0.1 mg/mL. Millimoles: mmol = mass (mg) ÷ molecular weight.

material.heading: Dose calculations
material.body: Volume to give = (dose required ÷ stock strength) × stock volume ('what you want over what you've got times what it's in'). Dilution: C1V1 = C2V2. Dose by weight: dose = mg/kg × body weight. Body surface area (BSA) is used for anticancer drugs. Clark's rule estimates a child's dose: child dose = adult dose × (weight in lb ÷ 150); Young's rule: adult dose × age/(age + 12). Infusion rate (drops/min) = volume (mL) × drop factor ÷ time (min).

topics.title: The Prescription and Dispensing
topics.summary: Parts of a prescription, prescription abbreviations, dispensing process and labelling.

material.heading: The prescription
material.body: A prescription is a written order from a licensed prescriber to dispense a medicine for a patient. Parts: superscription (patient's details, date and the symbol Rx — 'recipe', take thou), inscription (drug name, strength and quantity), subscription (instructions to the pharmacist, e.g. dispense 20 tablets), signa or transcription (directions to the patient — 'Sig'), and the prescriber's signature and details. Controlled drugs (e.g. morphine, pethidine) require stricter prescription requirements and registers.

material.heading: Dispensing
material.body: Good dispensing practice: receive and validate the prescription (legality, completeness, appropriateness, interactions, allergies), interpret it, prepare and label the medicine, perform a final check, and counsel the patient. A label should include the patient's name, drug name and strength, dose and frequency, quantity, date, pharmacy name and address, and warnings (e.g. 'may cause drowsiness'). Counselling covers what the medicine is for, how and when to take it, duration, side effects, storage, and what to do if a dose is missed.
keyPoints: Validate → interpret → prepare → label → check → counsel
Label: patient, drug, dose, date, warnings

topics.title: Sources of Drugs and Drug Nomenclature
topics.summary: Natural and synthetic sources of drugs, drug names and pharmacopoeias.

material.heading: Sources of drugs
material.body: Drugs come from plants (morphine from Papaver somniferum, quinine from Cinchona bark, artemisinin from Artemisia annua, digoxin from Digitalis lanata), animals (insulin formerly from pigs/cattle, heparin), minerals (iron, zinc, magnesium sulphate), microorganisms (penicillin from Penicillium, streptomycin from Streptomyces), chemical synthesis (most modern drugs, e.g. paracetamol) and biotechnology/recombinant DNA (human insulin, erythropoietin, vaccines).

material.heading: Names and references
material.body: Each drug has a chemical name (describes structure), a generic or non-proprietary name (International Non-proprietary Name, INN, e.g. paracetamol/acetaminophen) and brand or proprietary names chosen by manufacturers (e.g. Panadol, Emzor Paracetamol). Generic prescribing is encouraged for cost and clarity. Official standards are set in pharmacopoeias — British Pharmacopoeia (BP), United States Pharmacopeia (USP), International Pharmacopoeia — while formularies (e.g. the Nigeria Essential Medicines List, BNF) guide selection and use. The WHO Essential Medicines List guides national lists.

topics.title: Introduction to Dosage Forms and Routes
topics.summary: Classification of dosage forms, routes of administration and why formulation matters.

material.heading: Dosage forms
material.body: A dosage form is the physical form in which a drug is delivered. Solid forms: tablets (plain, film-coated, enteric-coated, sustained-release, effervescent, sublingual), capsules (hard and soft gelatin), powders and granules. Liquid forms: solutions, syrups, elixirs (hydroalcoholic), suspensions (insoluble solid dispersed — shake well), emulsions (oil and water with an emulsifier). Semi-solids: ointments, creams, gels, pastes. Others: suppositories and pessaries, injections, inhalers, eye/ear drops, transdermal patches. Enteric coating protects the drug from gastric acid or the stomach from the drug.

material.heading: Routes
material.body: Enteral routes: oral (convenient but subject to first-pass metabolism), sublingual/buccal (avoids first-pass, e.g. glyceryl trinitrate), rectal. Parenteral routes: intravenous (100% bioavailability, fastest), intramuscular, subcutaneous (insulin, heparin), intradermal (BCG, Mantoux), intrathecal. Topical and transdermal routes act locally or give sustained systemic delivery. Inhalation delivers drugs to the lungs quickly (salbutamol). Formulation affects stability, taste, bioavailability, onset and patient adherence.
